title: The All-Star Level System, Explained from Scratch (Levels 1–7)
description: What do the levels actually mean, how do athletes move up, and why does your gym keep saying 'she's not ready for Level 4'? The honest breakdown.
headline: The *level system*, explained from scratch.
sub: Level 1 through Level 7 — what they mean, how athletes move through them, and why 'she's ready to move up' is more complicated than it sounds.
toc: The seven levels at a glance
The age grid, and why it decides more than parents expect
The three skill tracks that don't move together
Reading a team name: level versus division
Prep, novice, and elite: parallel tracks at the same level
Why the same level looks different at two gyms

blocks.text: All-star cheerleading is organized into seven levels, and the level is the most consequential label attached to your child's season. It decides which skills her team may legally compete, who they compete against, how many hours a week she spends in the gym, how far the family travels, and what the year costs. Most parents meet the system as a verdict — *she's a Level 3* — when it is really a rules framework with a lot of machinery underneath it.

In the United States that framework is maintained by **USASF**, with **IASF** filling the equivalent role internationally. Their rules define, for each level, which tumbling skills, stunts, pyramids, and tosses are legal. Event producers build divisions on top of that shared definition, which is why a Level 3 team from one state can travel and compete meaningfully against a Level 3 team from another.
What a level actually is

A level is not a rank or a grade. It is a **legality envelope** — the set of skills a team may put on the floor. Anything above it is illegal for that team no matter how well an athlete performs it. Anything below it stays legal and available.

Two consequences surprise families. First, the level belongs to the **team**, not the athlete: a Level 5 tumbler on a Level 3 team tumbles Level 3 content, full stop. Second, the envelope is a ceiling, not a requirement — a team can compete at Level 4 while performing very little Level 4 content and break no rules. Whether that is wise is a scoring question.
The seven levels at a glance
Treat the age column as description, not rule; eligibility comes from the **age grid**.
The age grid, and why it decides more than parents expect

Each season the governing body publishes an age grid mapping divisions to eligible birth years. The specific years change annually; two structural points do not. Eligibility is tied to **birth year rather than age on competition day**, so an athlete does not age out mid-season. And divisions deliberately **overlap** — Youth and Junior share birth years, so gyms can build rosters instead of splitting athletes by birthday.

So eligibility can shift between seasons even though nothing about a child's skills changed. An athlete who spent a year as one of the oldest kids in Youth can find herself the following spring as one of the youngest in Junior, against athletes with two or three more years of growth. Coaches call this *aging up*, and it is a common reason a strong athlete lands at a level she thought she had cleared. The upper levels also carry **minimum ages**: Levels 6 and 7 are closed to young athletes regardless of skill, so a twelve-year-old with a double full has no Level 6 division to enter.

items: Ask which **birth years** are eligible for each team, not which ages — the translation is where errors happen.
Ask whether your child ages up this year, and whether the team in that division sits at a different level.
Check crossover rules before counting on two teams — events limit them and gyms charge for them.

blocks.text: Skill, not seniority, decides placement

Years at a gym do not entitle an athlete to a level. Neither does her friend group, her family's tuition history, nor last season's placement — regression happens after an injury, a growth spurt, or a year of patchy attendance. What gyms evaluate is a **current, demonstrable skill set**: standing tumbling, running tumbling, the role she fills in a stunt group, jumps, motions, and how it holds up under the pressure of being watched and scored.
"A level is a skills ceiling, not a rank. Placing an athlete above her skills does not accelerate her — it raises her injury risk and costs her the confidence she already had."

Gyms are also not neutral parties. Higher-level teams generally carry higher tuition, more choreography, more competitions, and more travel, so there is a **structural incentive pointing upward**. That does not make a gym dishonest — a mis-placed athlete makes the whole team worse. But 'she's ready to move up' deserves a follow-up: *which skills does she have, and which does that level need?* A gym paying attention answers in specifics, immediately.
The three skill tracks that don't move together
Parents hear 'level' and think tumbling, because tumbling is the visible, nameable part. Coaches track at least three tracks, and an athlete is rarely in the same place on all of them.
Tumbling

The slowest of the three to build. Progression follows a physical logic: **non-inverted** skills first, then **inverted with the hands supporting** (walkovers, handsprings), then **aerial rotation tucked**, then **extended**, then **twisting while flipping**. Every stage demands a rigid shape held in the air, which is why conditioning gaps surface as plateaus rather than as visible weakness.
Stunting

A group skill, scored as one. An athlete is assessed for the role she can fill: **flyer** (balance, flexibility, and the discipline to hold a position while other people move her), **base** (leg drive, grip technique, timing matched to a partner exactly), or **backspot** (height, strength, responsibility for the flyer's head and shoulders on every catch). A gym short on bases will place a competent base higher than her tumbling alone suggests — roster reality, not favoritism.
Jumps, motions, and performance

The least discussed and the fastest to improve. Jump height, hip flexibility, motion sharpness, and the ability to project to a judging panel are all coachable inside one season, and all are scored. An athlete stuck on a tumbling skill can still raise her value to a team substantially here in a few months — worth knowing when a placement has gone the wrong way.
How athletes actually move up

There is no standardized test, belt, or certificate. Movement happens almost entirely at **tryouts**, at the gym's discretion, most commonly in late spring. What does exist is credentialing on the *coaching* side: coaches are credentialed by level, so a gym needs appropriately credentialed staff to field a team at a given level. Asking which of your child's coaches hold that credential is reasonable and revealing.

Mid-season moves are rare for reasons of choreography, not politics. A routine is built onto specific bodies — stunt groups matched by height and strength, pyramid connections that depend on who stands where, formations counted to the beat. Swapping one athlete triggers a chain of rebuilds, which gyms absorb for an injury but not for a skill landed in November.

items: **Level 1 to 2** is the smoothest move — walkovers and a round-off back handspring are flexibility-and-technique skills more than power skills.
**Level 2 to 3** hinges on the handspring **series**: two connected without a step, needing enough power in the first to feed the second.
**Level 3 to 4** is the wall most families hit. A standing back tuck commonly takes several months to a couple of years to develop safely, and it is where fear becomes a real, trainable variable.
**Level 4 to 5** demands layout tumbling plus single-leg stunting at speed. Many athletes plateau here, where the sport starts sorting on athleticism as much as effort.
**Level 5 to 6** is the elite threshold — power for height plus air awareness to control rotation on two axes at once.

blocks.text: Reading a team name: level versus division
A team's full competitive name is a stack of independent labels, and only one is the level. The others define **who you compete against**, not what you may do.

items: **Age division** — Tiny, Mini, Youth, Junior, Senior, Open, set by the season's age grid.
**Size** — small or large, set by an athlete-count cutoff that varies by event, so a small team is not scored against one fielding twice as many stunt groups.
**Gender composition** — all-girl, coed, or all-boy, with coed split further by the number of male athletes.
**Level** — the only one of the four that changes what is legal on the floor.

blocks.text: So 'Senior Small Coed Level 5' is four statements, three of them about the bracket. When a parent asks why the team placed sixth, the division is often a bigger part of the answer than the routine. A thin division with three entries produces a podium finish that means little; a stacked division can produce a sixth place that is the best routine that team has ever hit.
Prep, novice, and elite: parallel tracks at the same level

Most gyms now run more than one track. The elite or full-season track is the traditional model: year-round training, outside choreography, and a travel schedule. **Prep** and **novice** programs run alongside at the same nominal levels with a deliberately reduced footprint — fewer hours, a shorter season, local events only, and often a restricted skills list.

The cost difference is real and substantial; prep commonly runs a fraction of an elite team's season cost, largely because travel is where all-star money actually goes. The trade-off is development speed — fewer hours means slower skill acquisition, so an athlete who starts in prep and later wants an elite team often needs privates to close a gap she did not create.
'Level 2 Prep' and 'Level 2 Elite' are not the same product. Compare practice hours, number of competitions, and how many require a flight and a hotel — not the level number.
Why the same level looks different at two gyms

The skills list sets a floor and a ceiling, and gyms occupy the space between very differently. A Level 4 team at a nationally competitive program typically runs **ceiling-level content across most of the roster**. A Level 4 team at a smaller program may be entirely legal while only a handful of athletes perform the top skills and the rest fill in beneath them.

Both are Level 4, and they will not score the same, because all-star scoring rewards **how much of the team performs the difficulty** rather than whether anyone on it can. That is why a child on a Level 3 team at a demanding gym can be doing harder work, in a deeper division, than a child on a Level 4 team elsewhere. Before accepting a placement — or judging one — ask concrete questions:

items: How many athletes on this team will actually perform the level's top tumbling pass?
How many practice hours a week, and how many are skill instruction?
How many competitions require travel, and what is the all-in season cost including choreography, uniform, warmups, camp, and fees?
Which division does this team compete in, and how deep is it typically?
What specifically would my child need to add to be considered for the next level?

blocks.text: Level is the label the sport hands you first, and it explains less than it appears to. The team's content, the division's depth, and the gym's weekly hours are what describe the season you are actually signing up for.
